( = <reference osisRef="Matt.20.17-Matt.20.28">Mt 20:17-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.31-Luke.18.34">Lu 18:31-34</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27159" type="x-p"/> Third Announcement of His approaching Sufferings, Death, and Resurrection (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.32-Mark.10.34">Mr 10:32-34</reference>).<div eID="gen27159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14075"/><hi type="bold">32. And they were in the way--</hi>on the road.<div eID="gen27160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">going up to Jerusalem--</hi>in Perea, and probably somewhere between Ephraim and Jericho, on the farther side of the Jordan, and to the northeast of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen27161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Jesus went before them--</hi>as Grotius says, in the style of an intrepid Leader.<div eID="gen27162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they were amazed--</hi>or "struck with astonishment" at His courage in advancing to certain death.<div eID="gen27163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and as they followed, they were afraid--</hi>for their own safety. These artless, lifelike touches--not only from an eye-witness, but one whom the noble carriage of the Master struck with wonder and awe--are peculiar to Mark, and give the second Gospel a charm all its own; making us feel as if we ourselves were in the midst of the scenes it describes. Well might the poet exclaim:<div eID="gen27164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27165" type="x-p"/> "The Saviour, what a noble flame<div eID="gen27165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27166" type="x-p"/> Was kindled in His breast,<div eID="gen27166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27167" type="x-p"/> When, hasting to Jerusalem,<div eID="gen27167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27168" type="x-p"/> He march'd before the rest!"<div eID="gen27168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27169" type="x-p"/> Cowper<div eID="gen27169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And he took again the twelve--</hi>referring to His previous announcements on this sad subject.<div eID="gen27170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and began to tell them what things should happen unto him--</hi>"were going to befall Him." The word expresses something already begun but not brought to a head, rather than something wholly future. <div eID="gen27171" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8a8c4b5b1c4aee59f4382246f89fc5c10b71290: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14076"/><div sID="gen27172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14076"/><hi type="bold">33. Saying, Behold, we go up to Jerusalem--</hi>for the last time, and--"all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of man shall be accomplished" (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.31">Lu 18:31</reference>).<div eID="gen27172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Son of man shall be delivered unto the chief priests and unto the scribes; and they shall condemn him to death, and shall deliver him to the Gentiles--</hi>This is the first express statement that the Gentiles would combine with the Jews in His death; the two grand divisions of the human race for whom He died thus taking part in crucifying the Lord of Glory, as Webster and Wilkinson observe. <div eID="gen27173" type="x-p"/>
entries.52338c73b46b7a582cc248f199763d852f234a27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14077"/><div sID="gen27174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14077"/><hi type="bold">34. And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again--</hi>Singularly explicit as this announcement was, Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.34">Lu 18:34</reference>) says "they understood none of these things; and this saying was hid from them, neither knew they the things which were spoken." The meaning of the words they could be at no loss to understand, but their import in relation to His Messianic kingdom they could not penetrate; the whole prediction being right in the teeth of their preconceived notions. That they should have clung so tenaciously to the popular notion of an "unsuffering" Messiah, may surprise us; but it gives inexpressible weight to their after-testimony to a suffering and dying Saviour.<div eID="gen27174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ambitious Request of James and John--</hi>The Reply (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.35-Mark.10.45">Mr 10:35-45</reference>). <div eID="gen27175" type="x-p"/>
entries.07bbea9c20f33071ba0778ed6ce7a6bca7ea4530: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14078"/><div sID="gen27176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14078"/><hi type="bold">35. And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come unto him, saying--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.20">Mt 20:20</reference>) says their "mother came to Him with her sons, worshipping Him and desiring," &c. (Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.27.56">Mt 27:56</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Mark.15.40">Mr 15:40</reference>). Salome was her name (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.1">Mr 16:1</reference>). We cannot be sure with which of the parties the movement originated; but as our Lord, even in Matthew's account, addresses Himself to James and John, taking no account of the mother, it is likely the mother was merely set on by them. The thought was doubtless suggested to her sons by the recent promise to the Twelve of "thrones to sit on, when the Son of man should sit on the throne of His glory" (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>); but after the reproof so lately given them (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.33">Mr 9:33</reference>, &c.) they get their mother to speak for them.<div eID="gen27176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire--</hi>thus cautiously approaching the subject. <div eID="gen27177" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d8aa41b1e693fa71c8d7ac1c18f16385b6474f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14079"/><div sID="gen27178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14079"/><hi type="bold">36. And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you?--</hi>Though well aware what was in their mind and their mother's, our Lord will have the unseemly petition uttered before all. <div eID="gen27178" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d5e944221bcc0174a914274ee60f83d9c783af2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14080"/><div sID="gen27179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14080"/><hi type="bold">37. Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory--</hi>that is, Assign to us the two places of highest honor in the coming kingdom. The semblance of a plea for so presumptuous a request might possibly have been drawn from the fact that one of the two usually leaned on the breast of Jesus, or sat next Him at meals, while the other was one of the favored three. <div eID="gen27179" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cf46e4d35e8a1e55d09ef3877b2fea28b639554: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14081"/><div sID="gen27180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14081"/><hi type="bold">38. But Jesus said unto them, Ye know not what ye ask--</hi>How gentle the reply to such a request, preferred at such a time, after the sad announcement just made!<div eID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">can ye drink of the cup that I drink of?--</hi>To "drink of a cup" is in Scripture a figure for getting one's fill either of good (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.13">116:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.7">Jr 16:7</reference>) or of ill (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Psa 75:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.18.11">Joh 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Re 14:10</reference>). Here it is the cup of suffering.<div eID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?--</hi>(Compare for the language, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.7">Psa 42:7</reference>). The object of this question seems to have been to try how far those two men were capable of the dignity to which they aspired and this on the principle that he who is able to suffer most for His sake will be the nearest to Him in His kingdom. <div eID="gen27182" type="x-p"/>
entries.13740804b8f51e3b9ee3cce19d9468b1e5f79bf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14082"/><div sID="gen27183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14082"/><hi type="bold">39. And they said unto him, We can--</hi>Here we see them owning their mother's petition for them as their own; and doubtless they were perfectly sincere in professing their willingness to follow their Master to any suffering He might have to endure. As for James, he was the first of the apostles who was honored, and showed himself able to be baptized with his Master's baptism of blood (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.1">Ac 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>); while John, after going through all the persecutions to which the infant Church was exposed from the Jews, and sharing in the struggles and sufferings occasioned by the first triumphs of the Gospel among the Gentiles, lived to be the victim, after all the rest had got to glory, of a bitter persecution in the evening of his days, for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. Yes, they were dear believers and blessed men, in spite of this unworthy ambition, and their Lord knew it; and perhaps the foresight of what they would have to pass through, and the courageous testimony He would yet receive from them, was the cause of that gentleness which we cannot but wonder at in His reproof.<div eID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Jesus said unto them, Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of; and with the baptism that I am baptized withal shall ye be baptized--</hi>No doubt this prediction, when their sufferings at length came upon them, cheered them with the assurance, not that they would sit on His right and left hand--for of that thought they would be heartily ashamed--but that "if they suffered with Him, they should be also glorified together." <div eID="gen27184" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8d3c177de0dfed7a68412d667e5071dcee35365: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14083"/><div sID="gen27185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14083"/><hi type="bold">40. But to sit on my right hand and on my left hand in not mine to give; but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared--</hi>"of My Father" (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.23">Mt 20:23</reference>). The supplement which our translators have inserted is approved by some good interpreters, and the proper sense of the word rendered "but" is certainly in favor of it. But besides that it makes the statement too elliptical--leaving too many words to be supplied--it seems to make our Lord repudiate the right to assign to each of His people his place in the kingdom of glory; a thing which He nowhere else does, but rather the contrary. It is true that He says their place is "prepared for them by His Father." But that is true of their admission to heaven at all; and yet from His great white throne Jesus will Himself adjudicate the kingdom, and authoritatively invite into it those on His right hand, calling them the "blessed of His Father"; so little inconsistency is there between the eternal choice of them by His Father, and that public adjudication of them, not only to heaven in general, but each to his own position in it, which all Scripture assigns to Christ. The true rendering, then, of this clause, we take it, is this: "But to sit on My right hand and on My left hand is not Mine to give, save to them for whom it is prepared." When therefore He says, "It is not Mine to give," the meaning is, "I cannot give it as a favor to whomsoever I please, or on a principle of favoritism; it belongs exclusively to those for whom it is prepared," &c. And if this be His meaning, it will be seen how far our Lord is from disclaiming the right to assign to each his proper place in His Kingdom; that on the contrary, He expressly asserts it, merely announcing that the principle of distribution is quite different from what these petitioners supposed. Our Lord, it will be observed, does not deny the petition of James and John, or say they shall not occupy the place in His kingdom which they now improperly sought:--for aught we know, that may be their true place. All we are sure of is, that their asking it was displeasing to Him "to whom all judgment is committed," and so was not fitted to gain their object, but just the reverse. (See what is taught in <reference osisRef="Luke.14.8-Luke.14.11">Lu 14:8-11</reference>). One at least of these brethren, as Alford strikingly remarks, saw on the right and on the left hand of their Lord, as He hung upon the tree, the crucified thieves; and bitter indeed must have been the remembrance of this ambitious prayer at that moment. <div eID="gen27185" type="x-p"/>

entries.c2fc26c3b2c8b4a06f75a9a6d695d3bdf56d216c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14088"/><div sID="gen27193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14088"/><hi type="bold">45. All My servants shall there be equal; and the only greatness known to it shall be the greatness of humility and devotedness to the service of others. He that goes down the deepest in these services of self-denying humility shall rise the highest and hold the chiefest place in that kingdom; even as the Son of man, whose abasement and self-sacrifice for others, transcending all, gives Him of right a place above all!" As "the Word in the beginning with God," He was ministered unto; and as the risen Redeemer in our nature He now is ministered unto, "angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto Him" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>); but not for this came He hither. entries.73813c4ffc8509174a411e26b7937ccda0a5b08e: <div eID="gen39490" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39491" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39492" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39492" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39491" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39493" type="x-p"/> The Pharisees question our Lord concerning divorce, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.1-Mar.10.12">Mar 10:1-12</reference>. Little children are brought to him, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.13-Mar.10.16">Mar 10:13-16</reference>. The person who inquired how he might inherit eternal life, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.17-Mar.10.22">Mar 10:17-22</reference>. How difficult it is for a rich man to be saved, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.23-Mar.10.27">Mar 10:23-27</reference>. What they shall receive who have left all for Christ and his Gospel, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.28-Mar.10.31">Mar 10:28-31</reference>. He foretells his death, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.32-Mar.10.34">Mar 10:32-34</reference>. James and John desire places of pre-eminence in Christ's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.35-Mar.10.41">Mar 10:35-41</reference>. Christ shows them the necessity of humility, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.42-Mar.10.46">Mar 10:42-46</reference>. Blind Bartimeus healed, <reference osisRef="Mar.10.46-Mar.10.52">Mar 10:46-52</reference>. <div eID="gen39493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39494" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39495" type="x-p"/> He arose - Κακειθεν αναϚας may be translated, he departed thence. The verb ανιϚημι has this sense in some of the purest Greek writers. See Kypke. Many transactions took place between those mentioned in the preceding chapter, and these that follow, which are omitted by Matthew and Mark; but they are related both by Luke and John. See Lightfoot, and Bishop Newcome.
entries.641f16b4f8721dd76cbf8f3ef91f780eec1d19e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39496" type="x-p"/> Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife? - See this question about divorce largely explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.19.3-Mat.19.12">Mat 19:3-12</reference> (note).
entries.9dd896a8dab187e30f5ee5916e1ba11c197a6fa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen39496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39497" type="x-p"/> And if a woman shall put away her husband - From this it appears that in some cases, the wife assumed the very same right of divorcing her husband that the husband had of divorcing his wife; and yet this is not recorded any where in the Jewish laws, as far as I can find, that the women had such a right. Indeed, were the law which gives the permission all on one side, it would be unjust and oppressive; but where it is equally balanced, the right being the same on each side, it must serve as a mutual check, and prevent those evils it is intended to cure. Among the Jews there are several instances of the women having taken other men, even during the life of their own husbands. Nor do we find any law by which they were punished. Divorce never should be permitted but on this ground - "The parties are miserable together, and they are both perfectly willing to be separated." Then, if every thing else be proper, let them go different ways, that they may not ruin both themselves and their hapless offspring.
entries.013659ce62ba16a6d2876977255ba9b7ceaba6d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39498" type="x-p"/> And they brought young children - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.19.13-Mat.19.15">Mat 19:13-15</reference> (note).
entries.6651b080236c0135a662e3c70eb07ad89df7f1cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen39498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39499" type="x-p"/> And he took them up in his arms - One of the Itala reads in sinu suo - "in his bosom." Jesus Christ loves little children; and they are objects of his most peculiar care. Who can account for their continual preservation and support, while exposed to so many dangers, but on the ground of a peculiar and extraordinary providence? <div eID="gen39499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39500" type="x-p"/> And blessed them - Then, though little children, they were capable of receiving Christ's blessing. If Christ embraced them, why should not his Church embrace them? Why not dedicate them to God by baptism? - whether that be performed by sprinkling, washing, or immersion; for we need not dispute about the mode: on this point let every one be fully persuaded in his own mind. I confess it appears to me grossly heathenish and barbarous, to see parents who profess to believe in that Christ who loves children, and among them those whose creed does not prevent them from using infant baptism, depriving their children of an ordinance by which no soul can prove that they cannot be profited, and, through an unaccountable bigotry or carelessness, withholding from them the privilege of even a nominal dedication to God; and yet these very persons are ready enough to fly for a minister to baptize their child when they suppose it to be at the point of death! It would be no crime to pray that such persons should never have the privilege of hearing, My father! or, My mother! from the lips of their own child. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.6">Mat 3:6</reference> (note), and on <reference osisRef="Mar.16.16">Mar 16:16</reference> (note).
entries.b3e1893e89c9ae809686ec4f17a680cf185afd9a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen39500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39501" type="x-p"/> There came one running - See the case of this rich young man largely explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.19.16">Mat 19:16</reference> (note), etc.
entries.65b42633a29507d9332f6c6983cc12f2d1dcf81c: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39502" type="x-p"/> Then Jesus, beholding him - Looking earnestly, εμβλεψας, or affectionately upon him, loved him, because of his youth, his earnestness, and his sincerity. <div eID="gen39502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39503" type="x-p"/> One thing thou lackest - What was that? A heart disengaged from the world, and a complete renunciation of it and its concerns, that he might become a proper and successful laborer in the Lord's vineyard. See <reference osisRef="Mat.19.21">Mat 19:21</reference>. To say that it was something else he lacked, when Christ explains here his own meaning, is to be wise above what is written.
entries.fb455aad466297f9839c83f086d9df85b3ba1231: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen39503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39504" type="x-p"/> And he was sad at that saying - This young man had perhaps been a saint, and an eminent apostle, had he been poor! From this, and a multitude of other cases, we may learn that it is oftentimes a misfortune to be rich: but who is aware of this? - and who believes it?
entries.d735a3e016fa72f99593624c6dcd48079fde6cd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen39504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39505" type="x-p"/> And the Gospel's - Read, for the sake of the Gospel. I have with Griesbach adopted ἑνεκεν, for the sake, on the authority of BCDEGHKMS, V, sixty others, and almost all the versions.
entries.0d4d7e0f492415d71d8965d5235a07e0bc624526: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen39505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39506" type="x-p"/> In this time - Εν τῳ καιρῳ τουτῳ, In this very time. Though Jews and Gentiles have conspired together to destroy both me and you, my providence shall so work that nothing shall be lacking while any thing is necessary. <div eID="gen39506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39507" type="x-p"/> And fathers. This is added by K, upwards of sixty others, Ethiopic, Gothic, Slavonic, Saxon, Armenian, Coptic, and in one of my own MSS. of the Vulgate. <div eID="gen39507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39508" type="x-p"/> Some have been greatly embarrassed to find out the literal truth of these promises; and, some in flat opposition to the text, have said they are all to be understood spiritually. But thus far is plain, that those who have left all for the sake of Christ do find, among genuine Christians, spiritual relatives, which are as dear to them as fathers, mothers, etc.; yet they have the promise of receiving a hundredfold often literally fulfilled: for, wherever a Christian travels among Christians, the shelter of their houses, and the product of their lands, are at his service as far as they are requisite. Besides, these words were spoken primarily to the disciples, and pointed out their itinerant manner of life; and how, travelling about from house to house, preaching the Gospel of the grace of God, they should, among the followers of Christ, be provided with every thing necessary in all places, as if the whole were their own. I have often remarked that the genuine messengers of God, in the present day have, as noted above, this promise literally fulfilled. <div eID="gen39508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39509" type="x-p"/> With persecutions - For while you meet with nothing but kindness from true Christians, you shall be despised, and often afflicted, by those who are enemies to God and goodness; but, for your comfort, ye shall have in the world to come, αιωνι τῳ ερχομενῳ, the coming world, (that world which is on its way to meet you), eternal life.
entries.d9f478811a9b8585df6de262f60d99794929c9d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen39509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39510" type="x-p"/> And he took again the twelve - Or thus: For having again taken the twelve, etc. I translate και for, which signification it often bears; see <reference osisRef="Luk.1.22">Luk 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.12.35">Joh 12:35</reference>, and elsewhere. This gives the reason of the wonder and fear of the disciples, For he began to tell them on the way, what was to befall him. This sense of και, I find, is also noticed by Rosenmuller. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.17-Mat.20.19">Mat 20:17-19</reference> (note).
entries.892dab7d9011c03e37c7957be672a31928faf25e: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen39510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39511" type="x-p"/> And James and John - come unto him - The request here mentioned, Matthew says, <reference osisRef="Mat.20.20">Mat 20:20</reference>, was made by Salome their mother; the two places may be easily reconciled thus: - The mother introduced them, and made the request as if from herself; Jesus knowing whence it had come, immediately addressed himself to James and John, who were standing by; and the mother is no farther concerned in the business. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.20">Mat 20:20</reference>.
entries.4de74c4d7c18fbd936b7f0af9c1d1836942ad321: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen39511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39512" type="x-p"/> In thy glory - In the kingdom of thy glory - three MSS. Which kingdom they expected to be established on earth. <div eID="gen39512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39513" type="x-p"/> And be baptized - Or, be baptized. Instead of και and η or, is the reading of BCDL, five others, Coptic, Armenian, later Syriac in the margin, Vulgate, all the Itala, and Origen. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.22">Mat 20:22</reference>.
entries.7c96536555f22135a6a986e26a31a627d765df6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen39513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39514" type="x-p"/> Is not mine to give - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.23">Mat 20:23</reference> (note).
entries.01a9a83d70ad38607070e387f019517bc26c9a90: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen39514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39515" type="x-p"/> When the ten heard it - See <reference osisRef="Mat.20.24-Mat.20.28">Mat 20:24-28</reference>.
entries.74074a8403c18009e52cacd93fdc0fcbc09e88f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen39515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39516" type="x-p"/> Blind Bartimeus - בר bar in Syriac signifies son. It appears that he was thus named because Timeus, Talmeus or Talmai, was the name of his father, and thus the son would be called Bar-talmeus, or Bartholomew. Some suppose υἱος Τιμαιου, the son of Timeus, to be an interpolation. Bartimeus the son of Timeus, ὁ τυφλος, The blind man. It was because he was the most remarkable that this evangelist mentions him by name, as a person probably well known in those parts.
entries.5d1484b6ffbac69fcdf427b75eb3c10414f47630: <hi type="bold">Verse 50</hi> <div eID="gen39516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39517" type="x-p"/> And he, casting away his garment - He cast off his outward covering, a blanket, or loose piece of cloth, the usual upper garment of an Asiatic mendicant, which kept him from the inclemency of the weather, that he might have nothing to hinder him from getting speedily to Christ. If every penitent were as ready to throw aside his self-righteousness and sinful incumbrances, as this blind man was to throw aside his garment, we should have fewer delays in conversions than we now have; and all that have been convinced of sin would have been brought to the knowledge of the truth. The reader will at least pardon the introduction of the following anecdote, which may appear to some as illustrative of the doctrine grounded on this text. <div eID="gen39517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39518" type="x-p"/> A great revival of religion took place in some of the American States, about the year 1773, by the instrumentality of some itinerant preachers sent from England. Many, both whites and blacks, were brought to an acquaintance with God who bought them. Two of these, a white man and a negro, meeting together, began to speak concerning the goodness of God to their souls, (a custom which has ever been common among truly religious people). Among other things they were led to inquire how long each had known the salvation of God; and how long it was, after they were convinced of their sin and danger, before each got a satisfactory evidence of pardoning mercy. The white man said, "I was three months in deep distress of soul, before God spoke peace to my troubled, guilty conscience." "But it was only a fortnight," replied the negro, "from the time I first heard of Jesus, and felt that I was a sinner, till I received the knowledge of salvation by the remission of sins." "But what was the reason," said the white man, "that you found salvation sooner than I did?" "This is the reason," replied the other; "you white men have much clothing upon you, and when Christ calls, you cannot run to him; but we poor negroes have only this, (pointing to the mat or cloth which was tied round his waist), and when we hear the call, we throw it off instantly, and run to him." <div eID="gen39518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39519" type="x-p"/> Thus the poor son of Ham illustrated the text without intending it, as well as any doctor in the universe. People who have been educated in the principles of the Christian religion imagine themselves on this account Christians; and, when convinced of sin, they find great difficulty to come as mere sinners to God, to be saved only through the merits of Christ. Others, such as the negro in question, have nothing to plead but this, We have never heard of thee, and could not believe in thee of whom we had not heard; but this excuse will not avail now, as the true light is come - therefore they cast off this covering, and come to Jesus. See this miraculous cure explained at large on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.29-Mat.20.34">Mat 20:29-34</reference>.
entries.68fcabebcd8074a933f29bb893230d4af0c07acf: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen39519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39520" type="x-p"/> Lord, that I might, etc. - The Codex Bezae, and some copies of the Itala, have, Κυριε ῥαββει, O Lord, my teacher.
entries.eb7a4370fa16a6a7edd98b67759e18339da43f20: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen39520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39521" type="x-p"/> Followed Jesus in the way - Instead of τῳ Ιησου, Jesus, several eminent critics read αυτω, him. This is the reading of ABCDL, fourteen others, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, later Syriac in the margin, two Persic, Vulgate, all the Itala, and Origen once. Jesus is the common reading; but this sacred name having occurred so immediately before, there could be no necessity for repeating it here, nor would the repetition have been elegant. <div eID="gen39521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39522" type="x-p"/> This very remarkable cure gives us another proof, not only of the sovereign power, but of the benevolence, of Christ: nor do we ever see that sovereign power used, but in the way of benevolence. How slow is God to punish! - how prone to spare! To his infinite benevolence, can it be any gratification to destroy any of the children of men? No! We must take great heed not to attribute to his sovereignty, acts which are inconsistent with his benevolence and mercy. I am afraid this is a prevailing error; and that it is not confined to any religious party exclusively.  <chapter eID="Mark.10"/> <div eID="gen39522" type="x-p"/>

entries.84aaca02167f6bdbefd7c4a92ae3dff2cfa8cca2:
Verse 16. Took them up in his arms. These were small children.

Blessed them. Prayed for them, sought a blessing on them, or gave them the assurance of his favour as the Messiah.

How happy would it be if all parents thus felt it to be their privilege to present their children to Christ! The question with a parent should be, not whether he ought to present them by prayer, but whether he may do it. And so, too, the question respecting infant baptism is not so much whether a parent OUGHT to devote his children to God in this ordinance, as whether he MAY do it. It is an inestimable privilege to do it; not a matter of mere stern and iron-handed duty; and a parent with right feelings will come to God with his children in every way, and seek his blessing on them in the beginning of their journey of life. Our children are given to us but for a little time. They are in a world of danger, sin, and woe. They are exposed to temptation on every hand. If God be not their Friend, they have no friend that can aid them in the day of adversity, or keep them from the snares of the destroyer. If He is their Friend, they have nothing to fear. The proper expression, then, of parental feeling, is to come and offer them early to God. A parent should ask only the privilege of doing it. He should seek God's favour as the best inheritance of his children; and if a parent may devote his offspring to God if he may daily seek his blessing on them by prayer--it is all that he should ask. With proper feelings, he will rush to the throne of grace, and daily seek the protection and guidance of God for his children amidst the temptations and snares of an ungodly world, and implore Him to be their guide when the parent shall be laid in the silent grave.

So, children who have been devoted to God; who have been the daily objects of a father's prayers and a mother's tears; who have been again and again presented to Jesus in infancy and childhood; are under the most sacred obligations to live to God. They should never forget that a parent sought the favour of God as the chief blessing; and having been offered to Jesus by prayer and baptism in their first days on earth, they should make it their great aim to be prepared to meet him when he shall come in the clouds of heaven.

Running. Thus showing the intensity with which he desired to know the way of life. Zeal to know the way to be saved is proper; nor is it possible to be too intense, if well directed. Nothing else is so important, and nothing demands, therefore, so much effort and haste.

Verse 19. Defraud not. Do not take away your neighbour's property by fraud or dishonesty. To cheat or defraud supposes a covetous desire of a neighbour's property, and is usually attended with falsehood or false witness against a neighbour in obtaining it. It is thus a violation of the ninth and tenth commandments; and our Saviour very properly, therefore, condensed the two, and expressed their substance in this--not to defraud. It is, besides, expressly forbidden in Lev 19:13--"Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour."

Verse 21. Jesus--loved him. What occurred afterwards showed that the young man did not love the Saviour, or was not a true disciple. So that this expression denotes, simply, natural affection; or means that Jesus was pleased with his amiableness, his morality, and his external regard for the law of God. At the same time, this was entirely consistent with deep sorrow that he would not give his heart to God, and with deep abhorrence of such a love of the world as to blind the mind to the beauty of true religion, and to lead to the rejection of the Messiah, and the destruction of the soul.

One thing thou lackest. When the young man came to Jesus, he asked him, "What lack I yet?" Mt 19:20. This question Mark has omitted, but he has retained the answer. The answer means-- There is one thing yet wanting. Though all that you have said should be true yet to make the system complete, or to show that you really are disposed to keep the commands of God, go and sell your property. See whether you love God more than you do your wealth. By doing that, you will show that your love of God is supreme; that your obedience is not merely external and formal, but sincere and real; the thing, now lacking, will be made up.

entries.11c1ac86ffc36bc3e3d0ae29625ef56e0f08f055:
Verse 30. An hundredfold. A hundred times as much.

In this time. In this life. In the time that he forsakes all.

Houses, etc. This cannot be taken literally, as promising a hundred times as many mothers, sisters, etc. It means, evidently, that the loss shall be a hundred times compensated or made up; or that, in the possession of religion, we have a hundred times the value of all that we forsake. This consists in the pardon of sin, in the favour of God, in peace of conscience, in support in trials and in death, and in raising up friends in the place of those who are left--spiritual brethren, and sisters, and mothers, etc. And this corresponds to the experience of all who ever became Christians. At the same time, it is true that godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that is, as well as of that which is to come. The favour of God is the security for every blessing. Obedience to his law secures industry, temperance, chastity, economy, prudence, health, and the confidence of the world--all indispensable to success in life, and all connected, commonly, with success. Though the wicked sometimes prosper, yet the surest way of prosperity is to fear God and keep his commandments. Thus will all needed blessings descend on us here, and eternal blessings hereafter.

With persecutions. Persecutions, or the contempt of the world, and bodily sufferings on account of their religion, they must meet. Jesus did not conceal this. But he consoled them. He assured them that amidst these, or perhaps it should be rendered "after" these, they should find friends and comfort. It is well to bear trial if God be our friend. With the promises of the Bible in oar hand, we may hail persecutions, and thank God that, amidst so many sorrows, he has furnished such superabundant consolations.

He threw it off, full of joy at the prospect of being healed, and that he might run without impediment to Jesus. This may be used to illustrate-- though it had no such original reference--the manner in which a sinner should come to Jesus. entries.eb0ed0a0f8b87537031ff5a4e2cebffe88bbf6fe: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.10.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.10.21" sID="gen100901" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.21">Mark 10:21</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">One thing thou wantest.</hi> Christ therefore does not mean that the <hi type="italic">young man wanted </hi>one <hi type="italic">Thing</hi> beyond the keeping of the law, but in the very keeping of the law. For though the law nowhere obliges us to <hi type="italic">sell all</hi>, yet as it represses all sinful desires, and teaches us to <hi type="italic">bear the cross,</hi> as it bids us be prepared for hunger and poverty, the <hi type="italic">young man </hi>is very far from keeping it fully, so long as he is attached to his riches, and burns with covetousness. And he says that <hi type="italic">one thing is wanting</hi>, because he does not need to preach to him about fornication and murder, but to point out a particular disease, as if he were laying his finger on the sore.<div eID="gen100902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100903" type="x-p"/>It ought also to be observed, that he does not only enjoin him <hi type="italic">to sell</hi>, but likewise to <hi type="italic">give to the poor; </hi>for to part with riches would not be in itself a virtue, but rather a vain ambition. Profane historians applaud Crates, a Theban, because he threw into the sea his money and all that he reckoned valuable; for he did not think that he could save himself unless his wealth were lost; as if it would not have been better to bestow on others what he imagined to be more than he needed. Certainly, as <hi type="italic">charity is the bond of perfection</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.3.14">Colossians 3:14</reference>,) he who deprives others, along with himself, of the use of money, deserves no praise; and therefore Christ applauds not simply the <hi type="italic">sellin</hi>g but liberality in assisting <hi type="italic">the poor</hi><div eID="gen100903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100904" type="x-p"/>The mortification of the flesh is still more strongly urged by Christ, when he says, <hi type="italic">Follow me.</hi> For he enjoins him not only to become his disciple, but to submit his shoulders to <hi type="italic">bear the cross,</hi> as Mark expressly states. And it was necessary that such an excitement should be applied; for, having been accustomed to the ease, and leisure and conveniences, of home, he had never experienced, in the smallest degree, what it was to crucify the old man, and to subdue the desires of the flesh. But it is excessively ridiculous in the monks, under the pretense of this passage, to claim for themselves state of perfection. First, it is easy to infer, that Christ does not command all without exception to <hi type="italic">sell all that they have; </hi>for the husbandman, who had been accustomed to live by his labor, and to support his children, would do wrong in selling his possession, if he were not constrained to it by any necessity. To keep what God has put in our power, provided that, by maintaining ourselves and our family in sober and frugal manner, we bestow some portion on the poor, is a greater virtue than to squander all. But what sort of thing is that famous <hi type="italic">selling</hi>, on which the monks plume themselves? A good part of them, finding no provision at home, plunge themselves into monasteries as well-stocked hog-styes. All take such good care of themselves, that they feed in idleness on the bread of others. A rare exchange truly, when those who are ordered to give to the poor what they justly possess are not satisfied with their own, but seize on the property of others.<div eID="gen100904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100905" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Jesus beholding him, loved him.</hi> The inference which the Papists draw from this, that works morally good — that is, works which are not performed by the impulse of the Spirit, but go before regeneration — have <hi type="italic">the merit of congruity</hi>, is an excessively childish contrivance. For if <hi type="italic">merit </hi>be alleged to be the consequence of the love of God, we must then say that frogs and fleas have merit, because all the creatures of God, without exception, are the objects of his love. To distinguish the degrees of love is, therefore, a matter of importance. <note n="627"> <div sID="gen100906" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Parquoy il est besoin de mettre quelque distinction, et recognoistre qu’il y a divers degrez d’amour en Dieu</foreign>;” — “wherefore it is necessary to state some distinction, and to observe that there are various degrees of love in God.”<div eID="gen100906" type="x-p"/> </note> As to the present passage, it may be enough to state briefly, that God embraces in fatherly love none but his children, whom he has regenerated with the Spirit of adoption, and that it is in consequence of this love that they are accepted at his tribunal. In this sense, to be loved by God, and to be justified in his sight, are synonymous terms. <note n="628"> <div sID="gen100907" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Signifient du tout une mesme chose</foreign>;” — “mean entirely the same thing.”<div eID="gen100907" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100908" type="x-p"/>But God is sometimes said to <hi type="italic">love </hi>those whom he does not approve or justify; for, since the preservation of the human race is agreeable to Him — which consists in justice, uprightness, moderation, prudence, fidelity, and temperance — he is said to <hi type="italic">love </hi>the political virtues; not that they are meritorious of salvation or of grace, but that they have reference to an end of which he approves. In this sense, under various points of view, God <hi type="italic">loved </hi>Aristides and Fabricius, and also <hi type="italic">hated </hi>them; for, in so far as he had bestowed on them outward righteousness, and that for the general advantage, he <hi type="italic">loved </hi>his own work in them; but as their heart was impure, the outward semblance of righteousness was of no avail for obtaining righteousness. For we know that by faith alone hearts are purified, and that the Spirit of uprightness is given to the members of Christ alone. Thus the question is answered, How was it possible that Christ should <hi type="italic">love </hi>a man who was proud and a hypocrite, while nothing is more hateful to God than these two vices? For it is not inconsistent, that the good seed, which God has implanted in some natures, shall be <hi type="italic">loved </hi>by Him, and yet that He should reject their persons and works on account of corruption.<div eID="gen100908" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.10.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100901" osisID="Mark.10.21" type="section"/>
entries.f3f0a4f5455876a25be98d75162f160aaf5e5e86: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.10.52" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.10.52" sID="gen101118" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.52">Mark 10:52</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thy faith hath saved thee</hi> By the word<hi type="italic"> faith</hi> is meant not only a confident hope of recovering sight, but a loftier conviction, which was, that this <hi type="italic">blind man </hi>had acknowledged Jesus to be the Messiah whom God had promised. Nor must we imagine that it was only some confused knowledge; for we have already seen that this confession was taken from the Law and the Prophets. For the <hi type="italic">blind man </hi>did not at random bestow on Christ the name of <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi>, but embraced him as that person whose coming he had been taught by the divine predictions to expect. Now Christ attributes it to faith that <hi type="italic">the blind man received sight;</hi> for, though the power and grace of God sometimes extend even to unbelievers, yet no man enjoys His benefits in a right and profitable manner, unless he receive them by faith; nay, the use of the gifts of God is so far from being advantageous to unbelievers, that it is even hurtful. And therefore, when Christ says, <hi type="italic">thy faith hath saved thee,</hi> the word <hi type="italic">saved </hi>is not limited to an outward <hi type="italic">cure</hi>,<hi type="italic"> </hi>but includes also the <hi type="italic">health </hi>and <hi type="italic">safety </hi>of the soul; as if Christ had said, that by <hi type="italic">faith </hi>the blind man obtained that God was gracious to him, and granted his wish. And if it was in regard <hi type="italic">to faith </hi>that God bestowed his favor on the blind man, it follows that he was justified by <hi type="italic">faith</hi><div eID="gen101119" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.10.52" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101118" osisID="Mark.10.52" type="section"/>

               <ns0:p n="18">18 And Jesus said unto him, Why callest thou me good? <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> none good, but one, <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> God.<ns0:note place="bottom">That is <ns0:hi>Originally good,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Supremely</ns0:hi> good, or <ns0:hi>perfectly good.</ns0:hi> Herein our Saviour doth not deny himself to be God, but check<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed him who did not believe him such, yet called him God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Thou knowest the commandments, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod 20.14. Rom. 13.9.</ns0:note> Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Defraud not, Honour thy father and mother.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And he answered and said unto him, Master, all these have I observed from my youth.<ns0:note place="bottom">That is, in that Latitude to which the <ns0:hi>Doctors</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Iewish Church,</ns0:hi> at that time expounded them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Then Jesus beholding him, loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest, go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 6.19. Luke 12.33. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 16.9.</ns0:note> treasure in heaven, and come take up the cross, and follow me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved, for he had great possessions.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.16, 17, 18. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Christ had an humane Compassion towards so Civil a Person, but sheweth him, that <ns0:hi>Love was the fulfilling of the Law,</ns0:hi> and that <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> is seen <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> a Resolution to yield an <ns0:hi>Vniversal Obedience</ns0:hi> to the Will of God. Our Saviour imposeth a special Precept upon him con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyned with two general Precepts concerning all the Disciples of Christ, to which his not yielding obedience, shewed that he was mistaken in his Notion, That he had <ns0:hi>from his Youth kept the Commandements,</ns0:hi> tho it might be true according to that Law-Interpretation of them given by the Pharisees.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 18.24, 25.</ns0:note> And Jesus looked round about, and saith unto his disciples, How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And the disciples were astonished at his words. But Jesus answereth again, and saith unto them, Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren, how hard is it for them that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 31.24. Psal. 62.10. 1 Tim. 6.17.</ns0:note> trust in riches, to enter into the kingdom of God?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, then for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And they were astonished out of measure, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing among themselves, Who then can be saved?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And Jesus looking upon them, saith, With men <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> impossible, but not with God, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 32.17. Luke 1.37.</ns0:note> with God all things are possible.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.23, 24, 25. where the same Hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />story occurred, and all the additions to it here are opened.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 19.27.28. Luke 18.28.</ns0:note> Then Peter began to say unto him, Lo, we have left all, and have followed thee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And Jesus answered and said, Verily, I say un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my sake and the go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spels,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 But he shall receive an hundred-fold, now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers, and children, and lands, with persecutions, and in the world to come eternal life.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 19.30. Luke. 13.30.</ns0:note> But many <ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> are</ns0:hi> first, shall be last, and the last first.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> 19.27.28. Our Saviour having blessed the Poor especially such a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> had stripped themselves of all for his sake, and the Gospels; <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> raised up hopes to himself, who had no Riches to tre<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> in, or have his Heart cleave unto, and had stripped himself of all that little he had to follow Christ. Christ assures him that neither he, nor any other that had done so, should by it lose <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>y thing, for tho in this Life they should have <ns0:hi>Persecutions,</ns0:hi> yet they should be amply rewarded in <ns0:hi>Value</ns0:hi> if not in <ns0:hi>Species</ns0:hi> in this World, and with infinite happiness, in the next.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And they <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 18.31</ns0:note> were in the way going up to Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem, and Jesus went before them, and they were amazed, and as they followed, they were afraid. And he took again the twelve, and began to tell them, what things should happen unto them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 <ns0:hi>Saying,</ns0:hi> Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of man shall be delivered unto the chief priests, and unto the scribes, and they shall con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demn him to death, and shall deliver him to the Gentiles.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him, and the third day he shall rise again.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.17. This is at least the third time, that our Saviour instructeth his Disciples as to his Passion, toward which he was now going, and that with such a readiness, that to the Amazement of his Disciples he led the way, and out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />went them. It is observable that Christ here describeth his suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferings more particularly then before. He tells them here that he should be first delivered to the <ns0:hi>Chief Priests and the Scribes,</ns0:hi> they should <ns0:hi>Condemn him.</ns0:hi> Then they should deliver him to the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> (such were the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pontius Pilate</ns0:hi>) they should <ns0:hi>Mock him, Scourge him, Spit on him, put him to death,</ns0:hi> but he should rise again the third Day. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> adds, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 33. <ns0:hi>They understood none of these, and this saying was hid from them, neither knew they the things which were spoken.</ns0:hi> How hardly do we believe what seems contrary to our interests? but we are to hear for the time to come. This Premonition was afterwards of use to them, they remembred the Words of Jesus, when the things were come to pass. Preachers Words are not lost, tho at present they be not believed, or hearkned to.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And James and John the sons of Zebedee come unto him, saying, Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us, whatsoever we shall desire.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 They said unto him, Grant unto us, that we may sit one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 But Jesus said unto them, Ye know not what ye ask, Can ye drink of the cup that I drink of? and be baptized with the baptisme that I am baptized with?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And they said unto him, We can. And Jesus said unto them, Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of, and with the baptisme that I am baptized withal, shall ye be baptized.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 But to sit on my right hand, and on my left hand, is not mine to give, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Vnless for whom it is prepared.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> but <ns0:hi>it shall be given</ns0:hi> to them for whom it is prepared.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 And when the ten heard it, they began to be much displeased with James and John.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.20. where we have the same History, with little or no Variation, only <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> tells us, that <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> did that by their Mother, which <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> reports as done by them in Person, but there is nothing more ordinary even in our common Discourse, then to speak of that as done by our selves, which is done by another on our behalf, at our Command, or Sollicitation, both the Evangelists agree in all the other parts of their Relation, and in the following Discourse also very much.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 But Jesus called them to him, and saith unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 22.25.</ns0:note> Ye know that they which are accounted <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>think good.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to rule over the Gentiles, exercise lordship over them, and their great ones exercise authority upon them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 But so it shall not be among you, but whoso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever will be great among you, shall be your mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ster.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:287" />45 For even <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 13.14. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.7.</ns0:note> the Son of man came not to be mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistred unto, but to minister, and <ns0:note place="margin">1 Tim. 2.6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.14.</ns0:note> to give his life a ransom for many.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.25. where we had the same al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />most <ns0:hi>Verbatim.</ns0:hi> Those that think it worth the while to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quire, what Critical Men say about that Phrase <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> which we Translate <ns0:hi>those that are accounted to Rule,</ns0:hi> may find it in <ns0:hi>Poll Sy<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>is Criticorum.</ns0:hi> When all is said, doubtless the <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> in <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and <ns0:hi>Lukes</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> signify the same Persons. And our Translators might as justifiably have Translated those Words, <ns0:hi>The Rulers, as those who are accounted to Rule</ns0:hi> (which is a Translation the <ns0:hi>Active Participle</ns0:hi> will hardly bear.)</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 <ns0:note place="margin">Luke 18.35.</ns0:note> And they came to Jericho, And as he went out of Jericho with his disciples, and a great num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />be of people, blind Bartime<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>s, the son of Timeus, sate by the high-way-side begging.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, and say, Jesus, thou son of Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid, have mercy on me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 And many charged him, that he should hold his peace, but he cryed the more a great deal, Thou son of David, have mercy on me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called, and they call the blind man, saying unto him, Be of good comfort, rise, he calleth thee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 And he casting away his garment, rose, and came to Jesus.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 And Jesus answered, and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="52">52 And Jesus said unto him, Go thy way, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 9.22. Chap. 5.34.</ns0:note> thy faith <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>hath sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved thee.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> hath made thee whole. And immediately he re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived his sight, and followed Jesus in the way.<ns0:note place="bottom">This History is a meer Narrative of a matter of Fact, in the Relation of which no difficulties occur, which stand in need of Explication. <ns0:hi>Matthew, Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> relate it, with but two considerable differences. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> mentioneth two Blind Men, the other two <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> but one. It is probable the one was the more remarkable, and his Father a Person of some Note, there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore he is mentioned, also, the other probably some obscurer Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> reports it done, <ns0:hi>when he came nigh to</ns0:hi> Jericho. <ns0:hi>Mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> as he went out of <ns0:hi>Iericho,</ns0:hi> but tho <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, that he sate Begging by the way, as they came nigh to <ns0:hi>Iericho,</ns0:hi> yet he doth not say the Miracle of his Cure was wrought then. It is most probable, that he followed Christ into <ns0:hi>Iericho,</ns0:hi> cry<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing after him, and also when he went out of <ns0:hi>Iericho,</ns0:hi> and that it was as he went out of <ns0:hi>Iericho</ns0:hi> (as <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> say) that our Saviour took notice of him, called him, and wrought the Cure upon him. See further the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.17.</ns0:note>
